Abdicate.definition: to give up a throne or duty.
Abdicate.fullDefinition: To abdicate is to formally relinquish a position of power, or more loosely to walk away from a responsibility one is expected to carry.
Abdicate.example: By leaving every difficult decision to her deputies, the director effectively abdicated her role as head of the institute.

Abet.fullDefinition: To abet is to encourage or help someone carry out an act, usually one that is illegal or improper.
Abet.example: The clerk was charged with abetting the fraud by quietly backdating the contracts.

Abhor.fullDefinition: To abhor something is to regard it with deep moral or physical revulsion.
Abhor.example: Although she abhorred violence, the novelist believed fiction had a duty to depict it honestly.

Abject.fullDefinition: Abject describes a condition of extreme misery or degradation, or behavior so humbled that it lacks any self-respect.
Abject.example: The memoir describes the abject poverty of the mill towns in unsparing detail.

Aboveboard.fullDefinition: An aboveboard action is conducted openly, without concealment or trickery.
Aboveboard.example: To reassure skeptical investors, the company insisted that every transaction had been aboveboard.

Abrasive.fullDefinition: An abrasive person or style rubs others the wrong way through bluntness or rough handling, much as sandpaper wears down a surface.
Abrasive.example: His abrasive style in seminars discouraged quieter students from offering their views.

Abrogate.definition: to abolish a law or treaty formally.
Abrogate.fullDefinition: To abrogate is to repeal or do away with an agreement, right, or law through an official act.
Abrogate.example: The new government moved to abrogate the trade treaty its predecessor had signed.

Absolve.definition: to release from guilt or obligation.
Absolve.fullDefinition: To absolve someone is to free them from blame, sin, or a duty they would otherwise be bound by.
Absolve.example: The inquiry absolved the engineers of responsibility, placing the fault instead on faulty materials.

Abstruse.definition: obscure because highly technical or theoretical.
Abstruse.fullDefinition: Abstruse ideas are hard to penetrate because they are dense, abstract, or remote from ordinary experience.
Abstruse.example: The lecture drifted into abstruse debates about set theory that lost most of the audience.

Accretion.fullDefinition: Accretion is growth or increase that occurs through the gradual accumulation of layers or small additions over time.
Accretion.example: The legal code grew by accretion, each generation adding rules without removing the old ones.

Acme.definition: the pinnacle of achievement or quality.
Acme.fullDefinition: The acme is the point at which something reaches its fullest development or greatest excellence.
Acme.example: Critics regard the late quartets as the acme of the composer's art.

Acrimonious.fullDefinition: Acrimonious describes exchanges or relationships marked by sharp resentment and hostility.
Acrimonious.example: After an acrimonious split, the two founders refused to appear on the same stage.

Adamant.fullDefinition: Someone adamant holds a position firmly and cannot be persuaded to yield, whatever the pressure.
Adamant.example: The senator remained adamant that the bill would not pass without stronger safeguards.

Adept.fullDefinition: An adept person has become highly competent at a task, typically through long experience.
Adept.example: She became adept at reading medieval manuscripts after years in the archive.

Adherent.definition: a loyal supporter of a cause.
Adherent.fullDefinition: An adherent is someone who follows and upholds a particular belief, leader, or movement.
Adherent.example: Even the theory's most devoted adherents conceded that the new data were troubling.

Adroit.fullDefinition: Adroit describes nimble skill, whether with the hands or in handling tricky situations and people.
Adroit.example: An adroit negotiator, he turned a hostile meeting into a productive one.

Adverse.fullDefinition: Adverse conditions or effects work against one's interests or well-being.
Adverse.example: The trial was halted after several patients reported adverse reactions to the drug.

Aegis.fullDefinition: To act under the aegis of someone is to act with their backing, guidance, or protective authority.
Aegis.example: The excavation was carried out under the aegis of the national museum.

Affected.fullDefinition: Affected behavior is adopted artificially to impress others rather than arising naturally.
Affected.example: His affected British accent struck his old classmates as faintly ridiculous.

Affinity.fullDefinition: An affinity is a spontaneous attraction to something, or a resemblance that suggests a shared origin or nature.
Affinity.example: The poet had a deep affinity for the austere landscapes of the north.

Affront.fullDefinition: An affront is an action or remark that openly offends someone's dignity or values.
Affront.example: Many scholars viewed the closure of the library as an affront to the town's intellectual life.

Aggregate.definition: a total formed from many parts.
Aggregate.fullDefinition: An aggregate is a whole made by combining separate elements, often considered collectively rather than individually.
Aggregate.example: In the aggregate, the small donations exceeded the gift from the single wealthy patron.

Aggrieved.fullDefinition: An aggrieved person feels wronged and harbors a sense of injury or injustice.
Aggrieved.example: Aggrieved tenants filed a complaint after the landlord ignored repeated requests for repairs.

Alienate.fullDefinition: To alienate is to make someone feel isolated or turn them away from a group or person they were once close to.
Alienate.example: The party's shift to the extremes alienated many of its moderate voters.

Allay.fullDefinition: To allay is to diminish or put to rest a worry, suspicion, or concern.
Allay.example: The results of the second study did little to allay concerns about the method's reliability.

Allegory.definition: a story with a hidden symbolic meaning.
Allegory.fullDefinition: An allegory is a narrative in which characters and events stand for abstract ideas, often moral or political ones.
Allegory.example: Many readers interpret the novel as an allegory of the rise of totalitarian rule.

Altruism.fullDefinition: Altruism is the disposition to act for the benefit of others even at a cost to oneself.
Altruism.example: Biologists have long debated how altruism could evolve when it lowers an individual's chances of survival.

Amass.definition: to gather a large amount over time.
Amass.fullDefinition: To amass is to accumulate a great quantity of something, such as wealth, evidence, or possessions.
Amass.example: Over four decades the collector amassed one of the largest archives of early photographs.

Amicable.definition: marked by goodwill and no discord.
Amicable.fullDefinition: Amicable relations or settlements are conducted in a peaceable spirit without bitterness.
Amicable.example: Despite their rivalry, the two labs reached an amicable agreement to share the data.

Amorphous.fullDefinition: Something amorphous has no clear form, structure, or boundaries.
Amorphous.example: The committee's mandate was so amorphous that no one could say what it was supposed to achieve.

Ancillary.fullDefinition: Ancillary describes something that supplements a main activity or system without being central to it.
Ancillary.example: The museum funds its exhibitions partly through ancillary revenue from the café and gift shop.

Anecdotal.definition: based on personal stories, not data.
Anecdotal.fullDefinition: Anecdotal evidence rests on individual accounts or impressions rather than systematic study.
Anecdotal.example: The claim was supported only by anecdotal reports from a handful of practitioners.

Anemic.fullDefinition: In its figurative sense, anemic describes something weak, pale, or disappointingly lifeless.
Anemic.example: Economists blamed the anemic recovery on a prolonged slump in business investment.

Animosity.fullDefinition: Animosity is a strong ill will that tends to show itself in behavior, not merely in private feeling.
Animosity.example: The animosity between the two factions made compromise on the budget impossible.

Antagonize.fullDefinition: To antagonize someone is to act in a way that makes them angry or turns them into an opponent.
Antagonize.example: The editor was careful not to antagonize the reviewers whose goodwill the journal depended on.

Antecedent.definition: a prior event that leads to another.
Antecedent.fullDefinition: An antecedent is something that comes earlier in time or logic and helps account for what follows.
Antecedent.example: Historians trace the movement's antecedents to the reform societies of the previous century.

Aphorism.definition: a terse saying that expresses a truth.
Aphorism.fullDefinition: An aphorism is a brief, memorable statement of a general principle or observation about life.
Aphorism.example: The essayist was fond of aphorisms, closing each chapter with a single sharp sentence.

Aplomb.fullDefinition: Aplomb is the assured composure a person displays when handling a demanding or awkward situation.
Aplomb.example: The young pianist handled the broken string with remarkable aplomb and finished the sonata.

Apologist.definition: one who argues in defense of a doctrine.
Apologist.fullDefinition: An apologist offers reasoned arguments justifying a belief, institution, or regime, often one under attack.
Apologist.example: Even the regime's apologists struggled to explain the sudden arrests.

Apoplectic.fullDefinition: Someone apoplectic is so furious that they seem barely able to contain themselves.
Apoplectic.example: The author was apoplectic when the publisher altered the ending without consulting her.

Apposite.fullDefinition: An apposite remark or example fits the situation especially well.
Apposite.example: The judge closed her opinion with an apposite quotation from the framers.

Apprehensive.fullDefinition: An apprehensive person feels uneasy or fearful about a future event.
Apprehensive.example: Residents were apprehensive about the effect the new highway would have on the neighborhood.

Arbiter.definition: one with power to settle disputes.
Arbiter.fullDefinition: An arbiter is a person or body whose judgment decides a contested matter, or whose taste sets standards for others.
Arbiter.example: For decades the magazine served as the chief arbiter of literary reputation.

Arbitrary.fullDefinition: Something arbitrary is decided by personal choice or chance rather than by any principle or system.
Arbitrary.example: Critics argued that the cutoff date was arbitrary and excluded deserving applicants.

Archetype.definition: an original pattern or typical example.
Archetype.fullDefinition: An archetype is the first form from which later versions derive, or a figure that perfectly represents a type.
Archetype.example: The wandering hero of the epic became the archetype for countless later adventure stories.

Ardent.fullDefinition: An ardent supporter or feeling is marked by warmth and intense commitment.
Ardent.example: An ardent defender of free speech, the editor published views she personally rejected.

Arid.fullDefinition: Beyond its literal sense of very dry, arid describes writing or thought that lacks interest, feeling, or imagination.
Arid.example: The report's arid prose buried its important findings beneath tables of statistics.

Arrogate.definition: to claim a power without justification.
Arrogate.fullDefinition: To arrogate is to seize or assume a right, title, or authority that one is not entitled to.
Arrogate.example: The council accused the mayor of arrogating powers the charter reserved for the legislature.

Articulate.definition: able to speak clearly and coherently.
Articulate.fullDefinition: An articulate person expresses ideas in a well-organized, readily understood way.
Articulate.example: The most articulate students were not always those with the most original ideas.

Artifice.fullDefinition: Artifice is skillful trickery or ingenuity, especially when used to deceive or to create an effect.
Artifice.example: The play's charm lies in its refusal of artifice; the actors simply speak to the audience.

Ascendancy.definition: a rise to a controlling position.
Ascendancy.fullDefinition: Ascendancy is the state of having gained power or influence over rivals.
Ascendancy.example: The ascendancy of the merchant class gradually eroded the nobility's political control.

Ascribe.definition: to credit to a cause or source.
Ascribe.fullDefinition: To ascribe something is to attribute it to a particular origin, author, or reason.
Ascribe.example: Scholars once ascribed the poem to Chaucer, but the attribution is now doubted.

Aspersion.fullDefinition: An aspersion is a remark that casts doubt on someone's character or integrity, often indirectly.
Aspersion.example: Rather than engage the argument, the critic cast aspersions on the author's motives.

Assail.definition: to attack with blows or words.
Assail.fullDefinition: To assail is to set upon someone vigorously, whether physically or with criticism, questions, or doubts.
Assail.example: The minister was assailed by questions about the missing funds.

Assimilate.fullDefinition: To assimilate is to take in information, people, or customs and make them part of a larger whole.
Assimilate.example: Immigrant communities often assimilated slowly, keeping their languages for generations.

Astute.fullDefinition: An astute person quickly grasps a situation and uses that understanding to their advantage.
Astute.example: An astute observer of markets, she sold her shares months before the crash.

Atavistic.fullDefinition: Atavistic traits or impulses recall those of remote ancestors, often suggesting something primitive resurfacing.
Atavistic.example: The novelist portrays the crowd's violence as an atavistic return to tribal instinct.

Atrophy.fullDefinition: To atrophy is to weaken or degenerate, as a muscle does when unused or a skill does when neglected.
Atrophy.example: Without regular debate, the society's critical faculties began to atrophy.

Attest.fullDefinition: To attest is to confirm or bear witness to the truth or existence of something.
Attest.example: The worn stone steps attest to centuries of pilgrims climbing to the shrine.

Augment.fullDefinition: To augment is to make something greater in size, amount, or strength by supplementing it.
Augment.example: The researchers augmented their survey data with in-depth interviews.

Autocratic.fullDefinition: An autocratic ruler or manner concentrates authority in one person and tolerates no challenge.
Autocratic.example: The founder's autocratic leadership left the board with little real influence.

Autonomous.fullDefinition: Something autonomous operates under its own rules or control rather than being directed by an outside authority.
Autonomous.example: The region became autonomous in 1979, with its own parliament and courts.

Averse.fullDefinition: To be averse to something is to be disinclined toward it or unwilling to accept it.
Averse.example: Risk-averse investors moved their savings into government bonds.

Badger.fullDefinition: To badger someone is to keep pressing them with requests or questions until they become worn down.
Badger.example: Reporters badgered the spokesman for details he was not authorized to give.

Baleful.fullDefinition: Something baleful carries a sense of menace or exerts a destructive influence.
Baleful.example: The essay traces the baleful influence of propaganda on public discourse.

Balk.fullDefinition: To balk is to stop short and be unwilling to go forward with something, often out of objection or fear.
Balk.example: Several donors balked at the cost of the new wing.

Bane.fullDefinition: A bane is something that causes continual trouble, distress, or ruin.
Bane.example: Invasive weeds have long been the bane of farmers in the valley.

Baroque.definition: elaborate to the point of extravagance.
Baroque.fullDefinition: Beyond the historical style, baroque describes anything excessively ornate or intricate.
Baroque.example: Her baroque sentences, crowded with clauses, demand patient readers.

Base.fullDefinition: In its GRE sense, base describes motives or conduct that are dishonorable, selfish, or contemptible.
Base.example: The biographer refuses to attribute the general's decisions to base ambition alone.

Bastion.definition: a place that firmly upholds a principle.
Bastion.fullDefinition: A bastion is a stronghold, literally a fortification, and figuratively an institution that defends a value or way of life.
Bastion.example: The university was long regarded as a bastion of classical learning.

Bathos.definition: an abrupt slide from lofty to trivial.
Bathos.fullDefinition: Bathos is the unintended comic effect produced when serious writing suddenly descends into the commonplace or overly sentimental.
Bathos.example: The poem's final couplet sinks into bathos, undoing the grandeur of the earlier stanzas.

Beatific.fullDefinition: A beatific expression or state radiates calm, joyful happiness, as if blessed.
Beatific.example: The painter gives the saint a beatific smile that seems untouched by suffering.

Befuddle.fullDefinition: To befuddle is to confuse someone so that they cannot think clearly.
Befuddle.example: The tax form's instructions befuddled even the accountants.

Behemoth.fullDefinition: A behemoth is anything of monstrous size or overwhelming strength, often an organization.
Behemoth.example: The small publisher was eventually swallowed by a media behemoth.

Beholden.fullDefinition: Someone beholden to another is under an obligation to them, often in a way that limits their independence.
Beholden.example: Critics worried that the senator was beholden to the industries that funded his campaign.

Belabor.fullDefinition: To belabor a point is to discuss or explain it far longer than necessary.
Belabor.example: Without belaboring the obvious, the author moves quickly to her more surprising claims.

Beleaguer.fullDefinition: To beleaguer is to trouble or harass persistently, much as an army besieges a city.
Beleaguer.example: The beleaguered agency faced budget cuts, lawsuits, and a hiring freeze in the same year.

Belittle.definition: to make seem small or petty.
Belittle.fullDefinition: To belittle is to make a person or achievement seem smaller or less worthy than it is.
Belittle.example: Early reviewers belittled her research as a mere catalog of trivia.

Belligerent.fullDefinition: A belligerent person behaves aggressively and seems ready to start a conflict; the word also describes nations engaged in war.
Belligerent.example: The witness grew belligerent under cross-examination and refused to answer.

Bellwether.fullDefinition: A bellwether is a person, group, or thing whose behavior signals what others will soon do.
Bellwether.example: The county has been a reliable bellwether, voting for the winning candidate in every election since 1960.

Bemoan.definition: to express regret or grief over.
Bemoan.fullDefinition: To bemoan something is to complain or lament about it, often at length.
Bemoan.example: Teachers bemoan the decline of handwriting, though few can prove it matters.

Bemused.fullDefinition: A bemused person is bewildered or mildly confused, not, as is often assumed, simply amused.
Bemused.example: The bemused audience could not tell whether the play had ended or merely paused.

Benefactor.fullDefinition: A benefactor supports a person, institution, or cause, usually with money or gifts.
Benefactor.example: An anonymous benefactor endowed the scholarship that allowed him to attend college.

Benighted.fullDefinition: Benighted describes people or eras regarded as ignorant or unenlightened.
Benighted.example: The reformers saw themselves as bringing reason to a benighted age.

Berate.definition: to scold angrily and at length.
Berate.fullDefinition: To berate someone is to criticize them harshly and loudly for a perceived failure.
Berate.example: The conductor berated the brass section in front of the entire orchestra.

Bereft.fullDefinition: To be bereft is to be lacking something one needs or once had, such as hope, a loved one, or a quality.
Bereft.example: The final draft was bereft of the humor that had enlivened the earlier versions.

Besmirch.fullDefinition: To besmirch is to damage the good name or honor of a person or institution.
Besmirch.example: He sued the newspaper, claiming the article had besmirched his professional standing.

Bifurcate.fullDefinition: To bifurcate is to divide into two parts or paths, literally or figuratively.
Bifurcate.example: After the war, the movement bifurcated into a moderate wing and a radical one.

Bilk.fullDefinition: To bilk is to cheat someone of what they are owed, often through a fraudulent scheme.
Bilk.example: The fund's managers bilked retirees out of millions before the scheme collapsed.

Blandishment.definition: coaxing words meant to win favor.
Blandishment.fullDefinition: A blandishment is a flattering statement or action used to persuade someone gently.
Blandishment.example: Neither threats nor blandishments could persuade the reclusive author to give an interview.

Blatant.fullDefinition: Something blatant is done openly and unmistakably, often without any attempt to hide wrongdoing.
Blatant.example: The study's blatant disregard for its own control group undermined its conclusions.

Bluster.fullDefinition: Bluster is aggressive or self-important talk that has little real force behind it.
Bluster.example: Behind the bluster, the delegation was eager to reach a deal.

Boisterous.fullDefinition: Boisterous describes people or gatherings that are noisy and energetic, usually in a cheerful way.
Boisterous.example: The boisterous crowd outside the hall made it difficult to hear the speakers.

Bonhomie.fullDefinition: Bonhomie is a friendly, genial warmth that puts others at ease.
Bonhomie.example: The ambassador's bonhomie disguised a shrewd and calculating negotiator.

Boon.fullDefinition: A boon is something that brings advantage or relief, often unexpectedly.
Boon.example: The digitized archive has been a boon to historians who cannot travel.

Bootless.fullDefinition: A bootless effort produces no result and serves no purpose.
Bootless.example: After years of bootless appeals, the family abandoned the lawsuit.

Bourgeois.fullDefinition: Bourgeois describes values or tastes associated with the middle class, often implying materialism or respectability.
Bourgeois.example: The young painters mocked the bourgeois comforts their parents prized.

Bowdlerize.definition: to censor by removing offensive parts.
Bowdlerize.fullDefinition: To bowdlerize a text is to strip out material considered improper, often weakening the original.
Bowdlerize.example: The school edition bowdlerized the play, cutting nearly every bawdy joke.

Brash.fullDefinition: A brash person acts with loud confidence and little regard for caution or tact.
Brash.example: The brash young economist challenged the panel's assumptions in his first public talk.

Bravado.fullDefinition: Bravado is a boastful display of confidence or daring that often masks fear or weakness.
Bravado.example: His bravado faded once the true size of the debt became clear.

Brazen.fullDefinition: A brazen act is committed openly by someone who shows no embarrassment at being seen.
Brazen.example: The brazen forgery was displayed in the gallery for months before anyone questioned it.

Breach.definition: a violation of a law or agreement.
Breach.fullDefinition: A breach is the breaking of a rule, promise, or contract, or a gap made by breaking through a barrier.
Breach.example: Publishing the letters without permission was a clear breach of trust.

Brevity.fullDefinition: Brevity is the quality of being brief, whether in time or in the economical use of words.
Brevity.example: The brevity of the treaty concealed the complexity of the issues it settled.

Brusque.definition: abrupt to the point of rudeness.
Brusque.fullDefinition: A brusque manner is short and offhand in a way that seems impolite.
Brusque.example: Her brusque reply discouraged further questions from the press.

Bulwark.fullDefinition: A bulwark is a defensive wall, or anything that protects against danger or decline.
Bulwark.example: An independent judiciary is often described as a bulwark against tyranny.

Bungle.fullDefinition: To bungle a task is to perform it so ineptly that it fails or is spoiled.
Bungle.example: The agency bungled the rollout, leaving thousands without benefits for weeks.

Buoyant.fullDefinition: Beyond its literal sense of able to float, buoyant describes moods or markets that stay lively and optimistic.
Buoyant.example: Buoyant consumer spending kept the economy growing through the winter.

Burnish.definition: to polish; enhance the luster of.
Burnish.fullDefinition: To burnish is to make something shine by rubbing, or to improve a reputation or image.
Burnish.example: The governor hoped the reform would burnish his credentials before the national campaign.

Byzantine.definition: intricate and scheming, like a maze.
Byzantine.fullDefinition: Byzantine describes systems or politics so complicated and devious that they are hard to navigate.
Byzantine.example: Applicants must navigate a Byzantine permitting process involving six separate agencies.

Cabal.fullDefinition: A cabal is a small, closed circle of people who scheme together, usually to gain political power.
Cabal.example: The novel imagines a cabal of bankers secretly steering the nation's affairs.

Cajole.fullDefinition: To cajole is to persuade through flattery, gentle pressure, or repeated coaxing.
Cajole.example: The organizers cajoled the reluctant scientist into giving the keynote address.

Calamitous.fullDefinition: A calamitous event or decision brings about severe loss, damage, or suffering.
Calamitous.example: The decision to drain the wetlands proved calamitous for the region's bird populations.

Callous.fullDefinition: A callous person shows an insensitive disregard for the suffering of others.
Callous.example: The official's callous remarks about the flood victims provoked national outrage.

Callow.fullDefinition: Callow describes someone inexperienced and lacking the judgment that comes with age.
Callow.example: The memoir looks back with amusement on the author's callow opinions as a student.

Camaraderie.fullDefinition: Camaraderie is the spirit of friendship and loyalty that develops among people who share an experience.
Camaraderie.example: The camaraderie of the expedition team helped them endure months of isolation.

Candor.fullDefinition: Candor is the quality of speaking honestly and directly, even when the truth is uncomfortable.
Candor.example: Reviewers praised the diarist's candor about her own failures.

Cant.fullDefinition: Cant is hypocritical speech full of moral or religious sentiment the speaker does not truly hold; it can also mean the jargon of a group.
Cant.example: The essayist had no patience for the cant of politicians who praised thrift while spending lavishly.

Capacious.fullDefinition: Something capacious has a large capacity, whether a space, a container, or a mind.
Capacious.example: Her capacious memory allowed her to quote entire chapters from novels she had read once.

Capitulate.fullDefinition: To capitulate is to stop resisting and accept an opponent's demands or terms.
Capitulate.example: After weeks of protest, the administration capitulated and restored the program.

Caricature.fullDefinition: A caricature represents a person or idea by distorting its most distinctive features for comic or critical effect.
Caricature.example: The critic's summary was less a fair account of the theory than a caricature of it.

Carp.definition: to complain in a petty, nagging way.
Carp.fullDefinition: To carp is to keep finding fault over trivial matters.
Carp.example: Instead of carping about minor errors, the reviewer engaged with the book's central argument.

Cataclysm.fullDefinition: A cataclysm is a sudden event, natural or social, that causes enormous destruction or change.
Cataclysm.example: The war was a cataclysm that ended four empires within a decade.

Categorical.fullDefinition: A categorical statement is made without qualification or condition.
Categorical.example: The spokesperson issued a categorical denial that any data had been sold.

Catholic.fullDefinition: In lowercase use, catholic means broad and inclusive rather than narrow or specialized.
Catholic.example: A reader of catholic tastes, he moved easily from medieval theology to detective fiction.

Cavalier.fullDefinition: A cavalier attitude treats serious matters with careless or arrogant indifference.
Cavalier.example: The company's cavalier handling of customer data drew a large fine.

Caveat.fullDefinition: A caveat is a cautionary note that qualifies a statement or flags a risk.
Caveat.example: The authors present their findings with the caveat that the sample was small.

Cede.fullDefinition: To cede is to hand over control of land, power, or a position to another, often formally.
Cede.example: Under the treaty, the empire ceded its coastal provinces to its neighbor.

Censorious.fullDefinition: A censorious person habitually condemns others and is quick to find moral fault.
Censorious.example: The censorious tone of the review seemed out of proportion to the novel's minor flaws.

Certitude.fullDefinition: Certitude is a feeling of complete certainty, sometimes held more firmly than the evidence warrants.
Certitude.example: The early theorists spoke with a certitude that later research did not support.

Chagrin.fullDefinition: Chagrin is the vexation felt after a humiliation, failure, or disappointment.
Chagrin.example: To the curator's chagrin, the prized painting was revealed to be a copy.

Champion.definition: to fight vigorously on behalf of.
Champion.fullDefinition: As a verb, to champion is to take up and defend a cause or person with energy and conviction.
Champion.example: She championed the rights of tenant farmers long before the issue was fashionable.

Charlatan.fullDefinition: A charlatan pretends to have knowledge or skill they lack, typically to gain money or status.
Charlatan.example: The physician denounced the tonic's inventor as a charlatan preying on the desperate.

Check.fullDefinition: In its GRE sense, to check is to hold back or stop the progress of something, as in checks and balances.
Check.example: Strict quarantine measures checked the spread of the disease within weeks.

Churlish.fullDefinition: Churlish behavior is rude and mean-spirited, especially in failing to show expected courtesy.
Churlish.example: It would be churlish to deny the debut novel its considerable merits.

Circuitous.fullDefinition: A circuitous route or argument takes a long, winding way rather than going straight to its destination.
Circuitous.example: The memo reached its conclusion only by a circuitous path through several digressions.

Circumlocution.definition: talking around a point, not to it.
Circumlocution.fullDefinition: Circumlocution is the use of many words where few would do, often to evade a direct statement.
Circumlocution.example: The official's circumlocution left reporters unsure whether he had admitted anything.

Circumscribe.fullDefinition: To circumscribe is to confine something within boundaries, especially limits on power or freedom.
Circumscribe.example: The new constitution sharply circumscribed the powers of the monarch.

Circumvent.fullDefinition: To circumvent is to avoid an obstacle or rule by clever or devious means.
Circumvent.example: Firms set up overseas subsidiaries to circumvent the export ban.

Clamor.fullDefinition: A clamor is a noisy outcry, often a collective demand or protest.
Clamor.example: The clamor for reform grew louder after the scandal broke.

Clandestine.fullDefinition: Clandestine activities are kept hidden, usually because they are forbidden or politically dangerous.
Clandestine.example: Dissidents circulated their writings through a clandestine network of printers.

Clemency.fullDefinition: Clemency is leniency shown by someone in authority, such as a reduced sentence or a pardon.
Clemency.example: The governor granted clemency to prisoners convicted under the repealed law.

Cloying.fullDefinition: Something cloying is so sugary, whether in taste or in feeling, that it becomes unpleasant.
Cloying.example: The film's cloying final scene undercut the restraint of everything before it.

Coddle.fullDefinition: To coddle is to treat someone with too much indulgence or protection.
Coddle.example: Critics argued that the subsidies coddled inefficient industries.

Codify.definition: to arrange into a system of rules.
Codify.fullDefinition: To codify is to organize customs, laws, or practices into a formal, written system.
Codify.example: The emperor's jurists codified centuries of scattered legal rulings.

Coerce.definition: to compel by threats or force.
Coerce.fullDefinition: To coerce is to make someone act against their will through pressure or intimidation.
Coerce.example: Witnesses testified that they had been coerced into signing the confession.

Cognizant.fullDefinition: To be cognizant of something is to have knowledge or awareness of it.
Cognizant.example: Planners must be cognizant of how new roads change patterns of settlement.

Coherent.fullDefinition: A coherent argument or plan holds together, with parts that fit and follow from one another.
Coherent.example: The essay offers no coherent account of why the reforms failed.

Cohesive.fullDefinition: A cohesive group or work has parts that stick together and function as a whole.
Cohesive.example: The coalition was never cohesive; its members agreed only on what they opposed.

Colloquial.fullDefinition: Colloquial language belongs to everyday speech rather than formal writing.
Colloquial.example: The translator chose a colloquial idiom to capture the characters' banter.

Collusion.fullDefinition: Collusion is a covert agreement between parties, usually to cheat or mislead others.
Collusion.example: Regulators found evidence of collusion among the three firms to fix prices.

Commiserate.fullDefinition: To commiserate is to share in someone's sorrow or disappointment by voicing fellow feeling.
Commiserate.example: Rival candidates commiserated with one another after the funding was cut.

Complacent.fullDefinition: A complacent person is so pleased with their situation that they overlook dangers or the need to improve.
Complacent.example: Years of easy victories had made the champion complacent.

Complement.definition: to complete or enhance by contrast.
Complement.fullDefinition: To complement something is to supply what it lacks, so that the two together form a better whole.
Complement.example: The field observations complement the laboratory results rather than replace them.

Complicit.fullDefinition: To be complicit is to share responsibility for a wrong, whether by active help or by silence.
Complicit.example: The report concluded that the auditors were complicit in hiding the losses.

Compromise.definition: to undermine or expose to danger.
Compromise.fullDefinition: In its GRE sense, to compromise is to weaken the integrity, safety, or reputation of something.
Compromise.example: A single contaminated sample could compromise the entire study.

Compunction.definition: a twinge of guilt that restrains.
Compunction.fullDefinition: Compunction is a feeling of uneasiness about doing wrong, often mentioned by its absence.
Compunction.example: The forger felt no compunction about deceiving the museum.

Concede.fullDefinition: To concede is to acknowledge that something is true or valid, usually after resisting, or to give up a contest.
Concede.example: Even her critics conceded that the experiment was elegantly designed.

Conceit.fullDefinition: Conceit is an inflated opinion of one's own worth; in literature it can also mean an elaborate, far-fetched metaphor.
Conceit.example: His conceit blinded him to the flaws his colleagues saw at once.

Concerted.fullDefinition: A concerted effort is one in which several parties act together toward a shared goal.
Concerted.example: Only a concerted international response could slow the decline of the fishery.

Concomitant.fullDefinition: A concomitant condition occurs alongside another, often as a consequence of it.
Concomitant.example: Rapid urbanization brought a concomitant rise in demand for clean water.

Concur.fullDefinition: To concur is to agree with someone or with a judgment; events that concur happen at the same time.
Concur.example: Most reviewers concurred that the second volume was weaker than the first.

Conflagration.fullDefinition: A conflagration is a vast blaze; by extension it can mean a large-scale conflict.
Conflagration.example: The conflagration of 1871 destroyed most of the city's wooden buildings.

Conflate.definition: to wrongly fuse distinct ideas into one.
Conflate.fullDefinition: To conflate is to treat two or more separate things as if they were the same, often causing confusion.
Conflate.example: The article conflates correlation with causation throughout.

Confluence.fullDefinition: A confluence is the meeting of rivers or, figuratively, the convergence of circumstances or influences.
Confluence.example: The revolution arose from a rare confluence of economic distress and intellectual ferment.

Congenial.fullDefinition: Something congenial suits one's tastes or temperament; a congenial person is agreeable company.
Congenial.example: She found the small college more congenial to her research than the large university.

Conjecture.fullDefinition: A conjecture is an opinion or conclusion formed without proof, based on partial information.
Conjecture.example: Without the missing letters, the poet's motives remain a matter of conjecture.

Connive.definition: to secretly permit or plot wrongdoing.
Connive.fullDefinition: To connive is to conspire with others or to look the other way while wrongdoing takes place.
Connive.example: Officials were accused of conniving with smugglers to move goods past the border.

Conscientious.definition: guided by a sense of duty.
Conscientious.fullDefinition: A conscientious person works carefully and thoroughly because they wish to do what is right.
Conscientious.example: A conscientious editor, she checked every citation against the original source.

Consign.definition: to hand over to another's keeping.
Consign.fullDefinition: To consign is to deliver something to someone's care, or to assign it to an undesirable place or fate.
Consign.example: The rise of streaming threatened to consign the corner video store to history.

Consonant.fullDefinition: Something consonant with a principle or fact is consistent with it.
Consonant.example: The new policy is consonant with the agency's stated commitment to transparency.

Conspicuous.fullDefinition: Something conspicuous attracts attention because it is clearly visible or remarkable.
Conspicuous.example: The report is conspicuous for what it omits about the earlier failures.

Consternation.fullDefinition: Consternation is a feeling of anxiety or shock, typically caused by something unexpected.
Consternation.example: The sudden resignation caused consternation among the firm's investors.

Construe.definition: to interpret in a certain way.
Construe.fullDefinition: To construe is to understand or explain the meaning of words or actions in a particular sense.
Construe.example: Her silence was construed as consent, though she later denied it.

Consummate.fullDefinition: As an adjective, consummate describes someone who has reached the highest degree of skill or a quality.
Consummate.example: A consummate diplomat, he could disagree without giving offense.

Contingent.fullDefinition: Something contingent will happen only if certain other events or circumstances occur first.
Contingent.example: The grant is contingent on the university matching the funds.

Contravene.definition: to act contrary to a rule or principle.
Contravene.fullDefinition: To contravene is to violate a law or conflict with a principle or claim.
Contravene.example: The regulation was struck down because it contravened the free speech clause.

Contrived.fullDefinition: Something contrived seems obviously planned or artificial rather than natural or spontaneous.
Contrived.example: Critics found the novel's happy ending contrived.

Conversant.fullDefinition: To be conversant with a subject is to have a working knowledge of it.
Conversant.example: Few economists at the time were conversant with the new statistical methods.

Convivial.fullDefinition: A convivial occasion or person is lively and friendly, especially around food and drink.
Convivial.example: The convivial atmosphere of the salon encouraged writers to share unfinished work.

Cordial.fullDefinition: Cordial relations are polite and friendly, though not necessarily intimate.
Cordial.example: Relations between the two rivals remained cordial in public.

Corollary.fullDefinition: A corollary is a proposition or result that follows directly from one already established.
Corollary.example: A corollary of the theory is that prices should fall as competition increases.

Corporeal.fullDefinition: Corporeal refers to the material body or to tangible things, as opposed to the spiritual.
Corporeal.example: Medieval mystics often treated corporeal needs as distractions from devotion.

Cosmopolitan.definition: worldly; at home in many cultures.
Cosmopolitan.fullDefinition: A cosmopolitan person or place draws on and feels comfortable with influences from many countries.
Cosmopolitan.example: The port's cosmopolitan population spoke more than a dozen languages.

Coterie.definition: a small, exclusive circle of people.
Coterie.fullDefinition: A coterie is a close group sharing interests or tastes, often appearing closed to outsiders.
Coterie.example: The poet's work circulated only among a coterie of admirers until after her death.

Countenance.fullDefinition: As a verb, to countenance is to tolerate or permit something, usually something objectionable.
Countenance.example: The board would not countenance any further delays to the project.

Coy.fullDefinition: Someone coy is deliberately vague or shy about committing to an answer or showing their intentions.
Coy.example: The candidate remained coy about whether she would run again.

Crass.fullDefinition: Crass behavior shows a gross lack of refinement or concern for others' feelings.
Crass.example: The crass commercialism of the festival dismayed its founders.

Credence.fullDefinition: To give credence to a claim is to accept it as believable.
Credence.example: New fossil finds lent credence to the hypothesis.

Credo.fullDefinition: A credo is a statement of the principles that shape a person's or group's actions.
Credo.example: Simplicity in design was the credo of the architect's entire career.

Crux.fullDefinition: The crux of a problem or argument is the essential issue on which everything else turns.
Crux.example: The crux of the dispute was who owned the rights to the original recordings.

Cryptic.definition: having an obscure or coded meaning.
Cryptic.fullDefinition: A cryptic remark or message is puzzling because its meaning seems deliberately hidden.
Cryptic.example: The composer left only cryptic notes about how the final movement should be played.

Culminate.definition: to reach a final, climactic stage.
Culminate.fullDefinition: To culminate is to arrive at the high point or conclusion of a process.
Culminate.example: Years of protest culminated in the passage of the civil rights bill.

Cumbersome.fullDefinition: Something cumbersome is awkward to handle because of its size, weight, or complexity.
Cumbersome.example: The cumbersome approval process discouraged small businesses from applying.

Cumulative.fullDefinition: A cumulative effect builds up gradually as each new increment adds to what came before.
Cumulative.example: The cumulative impact of minor regulations proved greater than any single law.

Curmudgeon.fullDefinition: A curmudgeon is someone, often older, who is habitually grumpy and resistant to change.
Curmudgeon.example: The columnist cultivated a reputation as a lovable curmudgeon who disliked all new technology.

Cursory.fullDefinition: A cursory examination is done quickly, without attention to detail.
Cursory.example: Even a cursory reading of the contract reveals several contradictions.

Cynosure.fullDefinition: A cynosure is a person or thing that attracts everyone's admiration or interest.
Cynosure.example: The restored cathedral became the cynosure of the city's tourist trade.
